rawInput.complaint: A 30-year-old woman with an 11-year history of chronic occipital headaches and a family history of cancer presented with a 1-year history of increasing difficulty with speech and reaching high notes when singing. She also reported progressive difficulty swallowing, left-sided facial spasms, left-sided hearing loss, tinnitus, and dizziness. On examination, she had deficits of cranial nerves VIII through XII on the left side. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the head revealed a 2.6 cm mildly enhancing soft-tissue mass causing scalloped expansion of the left jugular foramen, with intracranial extension into the cerebellopontine angle and extracranial extension into the carotid space. Subsequent magnetic resonance imaging showed a 3.8 × 3.5 × 3.5 cm dumbbell-shaped lesion with a “salt & pepper” appearance on T2-weighted images, avid postcontrast enhancement, mass effect on the left medulla and anterior inferior cerebellum, and obscuration of left cranial nerves VII through XII. The left cervical internal carotid artery just proximal to the petrous segment was asymmetrically narrowed, and the left internal jugular vein was not visualized.

cotDiagnosis.reasoning:
The chief concern is a progressively symptomatic skull base/posterior fossa lesion causing lower cranial neuropathies. The patient has a long history of occipital headaches, but over the past year developed worsening speech difficulty, inability to reach high notes when singing, dysphagia, left facial spasms, left hearing loss, tinnitus, and dizziness. These symptoms localize to the left jugular foramen/cerebellopontine angle region with involvement of multiple cranial nerves, especially IX, X, XI, and XII, and also VIII.

Salient positive findings strongly support a jugular foramen mass. Examination showed deficits of cranial nerves VIII through XII on the left. CT demonstrated a mildly enhancing soft-tissue mass with scalloped expansion of the left jugular foramen, plus intracranial extension into the cerebellopontine angle and extracranial extension into the carotid space. MRI showed a 3.8 cm dumbbell-shaped lesion centered at the jugular foramen, with a classic “salt & pepper” appearance on T2-weighted imaging and avid enhancement, indicating a highly vascular tumor. There was mass effect on the left medulla and anterior inferior cerebellum, obscuration of left cranial nerves VII through XII, narrowing of the adjacent left cervical internal carotid artery, and nonvisualization of the left internal jugular vein. This pattern is characteristic of a paraganglioma arising in the jugular foramen region.

Pertinent negatives/less supportive features for alternatives: there is no description of internal auditory canal-centered disease, which would favor vestibular schwannoma. The lesion causes scalloped expansion of the jugular foramen rather than hyperostosis or a dural tail, arguing against meningioma. The marked vascular imaging appearance (“salt & pepper,” avid enhancement, vessel narrowing, jugular vein obliteration) is less typical for schwannoma. The lesion extends both intracranially and extracranially in a dumbbell configuration through the jugular foramen, which is classic for glomus jugulare rather than a primary CPA tumor.

Differential diagnosis: First, glomus jugulare paraganglioma fits extremely well because these tumors arise at the jugular foramen, are hypervascular, show salt-and-pepper MRI signal, avid enhancement, jugular foramen expansion, and cause lower cranial nerve palsies with tinnitus/hearing symptoms. Second, jugular foramen schwannoma is plausible because it can produce a dumbbell-shaped jugular foramen mass with multiple cranial neuropathies and CPA extension, but it is usually less vascular and lacks the classic salt-and-pepper appearance. Third, meningioma could occur at the skull base and enhance strongly, but it more often causes sclerotic bony change or a dural tail rather than scalloped jugular foramen expansion and prominent vascular flow-void pattern. Other CPA lesions such as vestibular schwannoma fit the hearing loss/tinnitus/dizziness but do not explain the jugular foramen expansion and extensive IX-XII deficits as well.

Narrowing to a single diagnosis: the combination of jugular foramen epicenter, dumbbell morphology with intracranial and extracranial extension, lower cranial nerve deficits, tinnitus/hearing symptoms, avid enhancement, and especially the MRI “salt & pepper” appearance makes the most likely diagnosis a glomus jugulare paraganglioma.

differentialDiagnoses.supportingEvidence: Centered at the left jugular foramen with scalloped expansion, intracranial CPA and extracranial carotid space extension, multiple CN VIII-XII deficits, avid enhancement, and classic T2 “salt & pepper” appearance of a hypervascular lesion.
Can present as a dumbbell-shaped jugular foramen mass with CPA extension and lower cranial neuropathies, but the marked hypervascularity and “salt & pepper” MRI pattern are less typical.

differentialDiagnoses.condition: Meningioma of the jugular foramen/skull base
differentialDiagnoses.supportingEvidence: Could enhance and compress adjacent cranial nerves, but the lesion’s scalloped jugular foramen expansion, vascular imaging characteristics, and dumbbell extension pattern favor paraganglioma over meningioma.
